new_statements.quote: Finally, stress in Nyiyaparli is typical for an Australian language. Primary stress almost always falls on the first syllable of a word, characterised by an increase in loudness. Secondary stress usually falls on every odd-numbered syllable. The last syllable that would receive secondary stress may optionally be unstressed. The examples in (2.3) illustrate this pattern. (2.3) a. ˈkantiˌpurrku 'mob' ... b. ˈintinˌmalpi 'rain-PST' ... c. ˈthungkuˌwayiˌlakaˌlay 'cooked-INCH-when' ... d. ˈnyupaˌngarniˌthakuru 'spouse-PROP-CAUS-SIM=now'
new_statements.citation: Battin, Jacqueline. 2019. Topics in Nyiyaparli morphosyntax. Honours thesis, Australian National University. hdl:1885/209187

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the word-initial syllable (impressionistic, cued by loudness; 'almost always'); secondary stresses on subsequent odd-numbered syllables counting from the left (3rd, 5th..), i.e. left-to-right trochaic alternation; a word-final syllable that would carry secondary stress may surface unstressed (ex. 2.3d nyupa-ngarni-thakuru with no stress on the 7th syllable, vs 2.3c thungku-wayi-laka-lay with stress on final 'lay').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Usually on every odd-numbered syllable after the first; the last such syllable optionally unstressed.
new_statements.exceptions: Hedged as 'almost always' initial; no lexical exceptions listed. Author notes the phonology chapter is a brief overview (thesis focus is morphosyntax) and that phonetic/phonological topics need further research; description is impressionistic, based on von Brandenstein's 1960s recordings and 2019 fieldwork with David Stock.
new_statements.domain_note: Stated for the (grammatical) word; the examples include multiply suffixed words and one with an enclitic (=now), stressed as a single domain counting from the word-initial syllable. No separate statement about phrase-level prominence or citation forms.
new_statements.identity_note: nija1242 'Nijadali' [nad] is a Glottolog bookkeeping languoid: ISO 639-3 retired nad on 2016-01-15 (CR 2015-028) as a duplicate of xny Nyiyaparli. The real language-level entry is nija1241 'Nyiyaparli-Palyku' (Pama-Nyungan > Ngayarta/Pilbara; AIATSIS A50; also in our source list as a separate key with the same 'source-named-unreachable' scan classification). Battin 2019 describes Nyiyaparli as spoken by Nyiyaparli and Palyku people (treated as one language, 'Nyiyaparli/Palyku'), data from Gordon Mackay (von Brandenstein recordings, 1960s), Charlie Stream (Kohn fieldnotes 1995-2004) and David Stock (2019). Any catalog row should be filed under nija1241, not the retired nija1242.

new_statements.quote: Word stress is usually on the first syllable, so it is the first part of the word that sounds the loudest. For example, in the English word 'radio', stress occurs on the first part of the word 'radio', in 'retire' stress occurs in the second part of the word.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Blanket statement for the Western Australian languages covered by the handbook: primary stress on the first syllable. The Nyiyaparli-specific entry contains no phonological or stress information at all (names, classification, dialects, speaker numbers, word lists, and a bibliography of Brandenstein's unpublished materials).
new_statements.exceptions: none; the statement is hedged with 'usually' and is not language-specific
new_statements.identity_note: nija1242 'Nijadali' is a Glottolog bookkeeping entry: ISO code nad was retired on 2016-01-15 (change request 2015-028) as a duplicate of xny Nyiyaparli, i.e. the same language as Glottolog nija1241 Nyiyaparli-Palyku. Thieberger's handbook lists Nyiyaparli (sec. 4.5.6, with the spellings Iabali, Janari, Niabali, Njijabali, Njijapali, Nyiyabali, Nyiyapali) and Palyku (sec. 4.5.7) as separate entries but reports Brandenstein's view that Nyiyaparli is a dialect of Palyku. Battin 2019 (the existing statement) describes Nyiyaparli as spoken today in the Pilbara. No source distinguishes a 'Nijadali' variety with its own stress pattern.
